wine.name: Te Mata Coleraine
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, usually the larger part, with Merlot and a little Cabernet Franc; the blend moves with each vintage.
wine.sites: Chosen parcels of the estate's oldest vineyards in the Havelock Hills, on north facing, free draining slopes below Te Mata Peak, which the house tells as first planted in 1892.
wine.making: Each parcel is picked and fermented apart, and only the lots judged right for Coleraine are chosen for the blend. The wine is then aged in French oak barriques, mostly new, for around a year and a half before bottling.
wine.glass: Cassis, blackcurrant leaf and cedar over pencil shavings and a gravelly, graphite edge; medium in weight and moderate in alcohol, with fine, firm tannin and fresh acidity that keep it taut rather than ripe and broad.
wine.ageing: Closed and firm for its first eight to ten years in a strong vintage, it then opens slowly and can last for two decades and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The wine's name, taken from the town in Northern Ireland from which one founding family came.
The Geographical Indication of the North Island's east coast region around Napier and Hastings.
The house at Havelock North, named for the peak that stands above its vineyards.

records.table: Coleraine is Te Mata Estate's red from the old Havelock Hills vineyards, a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc first made in 1982. Cedar, cassis and firm, fine tannin; give it years in bottle and an hour in a decanter.
records.story: Bernard Chambers (1859 to 1931), a sheep farmer born at Te Mata, began to plant vines on the family's land in 1892, with Pinot Noir cuttings among the first, and by the account of the national encyclopedia he had made his first wine by 1895. The house counts 1896 as its founding. By 1910 Te Mata was, on the same account, the largest wine producer in New Zealand, but prohibition campaigns, pests, frost and the loss of workers in the First World War wore it down, and in 1917 Chambers sold the winery and most of the vineyard. For decades the estate made little of note. In 1974 two families bought it and set about restoring the old buildings and vines. Their first Coleraine came with the 1982 vintage, named for the Northern Irish town an ancestor of one family came from. In 2017 the British magazine Decanter named the 1998 Coleraine one of its Wine Legends, the first New Zealand wine it so named. For a sommelier, Coleraine is the reference for the Hawke's Bay Bordeaux blend: restrained, cedar framed and built to age.

Coleraine comes from the Havelock Hills, not from the Gimblett Gravels: Te Mata's oldest vineyards lie on the slopes below Te Mata Peak.

report: Founded follows the library's 1896; Te Ara gives the first vines in 1892 and the first wine by March 1895, and the house's own pages count 1896.
The sale of the winery is 1917 in Te Ara and 1919 in Wikipedia; the record follows Te Ara. The revival is 1974 in Te Ara and the house's page, 1978 in one merchant's profile, so 1974 stands.
The library's note that Coleraine is made only in the better years was not confirmed and is not repeated; the record says nothing of a vintage policy.
The barrel time is around a year and a half because the vintage notes read give 17 to 20 months, mostly new French oak.
The families who revived the estate are living in part and are never named.
The architect of the winery's extension in the 1980s and the single old vineyard of the first Coleraines rest on one source each and are left out.

wine.name: Craggy Range Le Sol Syrah
wine.sites: The house's Gimblett Gravels vineyard west of Hastings, bought and first planted in 1998, on greywacke stones with layers of silt and sand, inland and sheltered from the cooling sea breeze.
wine.making: The blocks are fermented apart with native yeast and a share of whole bunches that changes with the vintage, in recent years in French oak, concrete and wooden vats, with some three weeks on the skins. The wine is then raised for around a year and a half in French and Austrian oak barriques and puncheons, a minority new.
wine.glass: Blackberry, plum and violet over black pepper and graphite, with a smoky, savoury edge from the whole bunches; medium to full bodied, fine grained tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: More open on release than it once was, it gains savoury depth over a decade, and the house expects a strong vintage to keep for fifteen years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large Syrah or Burgundy glass.

records.table: Le Sol is Craggy Range's Syrah from its own vineyard on the Gimblett Gravels, first made in 2001. Blackberry, violet and black pepper over fine tannin: a cool climate Syrah closer to the northern Rhône than to the Barossa.
records.story: Craggy Range was founded in 1998 by an Australian family with a Master of Wine as its partner in the venture, by the house's own account. That year it bought a stony block on the Gimblett Gravels, the old bed of the Ngaruroro River west of Hastings, and began to plant it; a vineyard at Te Muna Road in Martinborough followed for Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc, and the cellar door was built near Havelock North. The first commercial vintage was 2001, and with it came the three reds the house built its name on: Le Sol from Syrah, Sophia from Merlot and The Quarry from Cabernet Sauvignon. In the same year, 2001, the growers of the Gimblett Gravels formed their own association and defined their district by its soil rather than by a line on a map, a step the association believes was a first for the New World. Le Sol has since become one of the wines a sommelier reaches for to show what Syrah can do on those stones: peppered, perfumed and fresher than its warm Australian cousins.

traps: Gimblett Gravels is a soil defined district trademarked by its growers' association, not a statutory appellation; the Geographical Indication on the label is Hawke's Bay.
Le Sol is Syrah and Sophia is Merlot led: the house's Pinot Noir comes from Te Muna Road in Martinborough, not from Hawke's Bay.

wine.name: Mission Jewelstone Syrah
wine.sites: The house's Mere Road vineyard on the Gimblett Gravels, west of Hastings, where a thin skin of sandy loam lies over the old river gravel.
wine.making: The grapes are partly crushed and fermented warm in small batches. The wine is then aged for about a year in French oak barrels, around a third of them new, before it is blended and bottled.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black cherry and black pepper with mocha and roasted chestnut from the oak, and a flinty, smoky edge; rich and concentrated, with ripe, fine tannin.
wine.ageing: Generous on release, it fills out over five to ten years and holds well beyond that in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large Syrah glass.

records.table: Mission Estate Winery is told as New Zealand's oldest surviving winery, begun by Marist missionaries in 1851. Its Jewelstone Syrah comes from the Mere Road vineyard on the Gimblett Gravels: blackberry, pepper and mocha, rich and supple.
records.story: The Catholic Marist mission came to Hawke's Bay from the north and planted its first vines at Pakowhai in 1851, chiefly to make wine for the Mass and the table; the winery counts that year as its founding, and the national encyclopedia names it the country's oldest surviving winemaker. In 1858 the mission moved some five kilometres to Meeanee, carrying its cottage with it, and there it built a seminary and kept its vines for half a century. Floods on the plain drove it out, and the brothers moved to higher ground at Greenmeadows in Taradale; in 1911, as the house tells it, their great wooden seminary was sawn into eleven pieces and carried there, where it stands as the winery's home. Wine was sold beyond the mission from the late nineteenth century, by the house's account under a French brother trained in the Loire, whose name its Huchet range carries. Syrah from the Gimblett Gravels later became one of its strengths. Jewelstone is the small batch tier the house sets just below Huchet; for a sommelier the Jewelstone Syrah is the way to pour a living piece of New Zealand's earliest wine history.

others.note: The house's highest range, made only in exceptional years and named for the nineteenth century cellar master of the mission.

traps: Mission Estate's seminary building stands at Greenmeadows in Taradale; the first vines of 1851 were planted at Pakowhai, and the mission moved to Meeanee in 1858.
Jewelstone is not the house's highest range: the Huchet wines, made only in exceptional years, stand above it.

The record is written for Jewelstone as plan.json asks and says plainly where it stands.

The 1897 purchase of the Taradale land rests on a Wikipedia talk page only and is left out.

Brother Cyprian Huchet's dates were not found in two sources (the house gives his arrival as 1871, another account a cellar tenure of 1870 to 1899), so he is described and named only through the range that carries his name.
The founding priest is named as Father Lampila in one account only and is not named.
The seminary left for Auckland in the 1990s by one account; with no second source the story does not say so.

wine.name: Trinity Hill Homage Syrah
wine.grapes: Syrah, with in some years a very small share of Viognier fermented with it.
wine.sites: The estate's oldest Syrah plantings on the Gimblett Gravels, propagated from Hermitage cuttings, from parcels such as Gimblett Stones and Roy's Hill.
wine.making: The grapes are picked by hand and fermented in small open vats, plunged by hand, with some parcels left as whole bunches and some, in some years, fermented with Viognier skins. The wine is aged in French oak, barriques with a good share new and in some years large ovals, for well over a year, and bottled with little or no fining.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black plum and violet over cracked pepper, smoked meat and a floral lift; dense yet fresh, with firm, fine grained tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Tight for its first five to eight years, it is made for the long term, and the house says a strong vintage can be kept for twenty years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a large Syrah glass.

records.table: Homage is Trinity Hill's Syrah from the Gimblett Gravels, first made in 2002 and only in strong years, from vines grown from Hermitage cuttings. Blackberry, violet and pepper, dense and firm: decant it, and pour it as the region's answer to the northern Rhône.
records.story: Trinity Hill was founded in 1993, when its partners planted vines on a barren plot of the old Ngaruroro riverbed off Gimblett Road, among the early growers on what came to be called the Gimblett Gravels. The house's first Syrah went in during the mid 1990s. After the harvest of 1996, which the founding winemaker worked at Paul Jaboulet Aîné in Hermitage, the Jaboulet family gave him Syrah cuttings from the hill of Hermitage, and Viognier from Côte-Rôtie came with them, as the house tells it. The vines passed through quarantine, were propagated and planted on the estate, and from them came Homage, first made with the 2002 vintage and named as a tribute to the Rhône house that gave them. It is made only in years the house judges strong enough, in small amounts, and was soon one of the wines that drew attention to Gimblett Gravels Syrah abroad. For a sommelier, Homage is the clearest lesson in the Rhône roots of Hawke's Bay Syrah: vines from Hermitage, fermented in the northern manner, grown on New Zealand river stones.

The source of the cuttings is the hill of Hermitage in two accounts; neither says La Chapelle, so the record says only Hermitage. Whether cuttings or budwood, and the planting year of 2002 given by one account, are left out.
The first Syrah planting is 1995 with a first Syrah wine of 1997 in one blog, so the story says the mid 1990s only.

wine.name: Church Road TOM Cabernet Sauvignon Merlot
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, usually the larger part, with Merlot; the balance moves with each vintage.
wine.sites: The house's Redstone vineyard in the Bridge Pa Triangle and its vineyards on the Gimblett Gravels, both on warm, free draining soils of the old river plain.
wine.making: The parcels are fermented apart, the Cabernet Sauvignon in some years in large French oak vats and the Merlot in stainless steel. The wine is then aged in French oak barriques, a large share new, for around a year and a half, and only in years the house judges exceptional.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant, plum and cedar with cocoa and toasted, nutty oak; full and fleshy, with supple yet firm tannin and a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and oaky in youth, it wants eight to ten years in a strong vintage and can last for two decades or more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: TOM is Church Road's Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, first made in 1995 and only in exceptional years, named for Tom McDonald, who made the cellar's name. Blackcurrant, cedar and firm, supple tannin; give it time and a decanter.
records.story: The winery on Church Road in Taradale was founded in 1897 by a settler from Luxembourg, on land beside the Marist mission. When he went back to Europe, a local boy who had worked in the cellar, Tom McDonald (1907 to 1987), took over the lease and in 1927, aged nineteen, bought the business. Through prohibition campaigns and the lean years that followed he kept it alive, building a new winery on Church Road in 1948, and in 1949 he made a Cabernet Sauvignon that is told as one of New Zealand's first commercial wines of the grape. In 1962 his firm merged with McWilliam's. Montana bought the Taradale winery in the late 1980s, renovated it and named it Church Road, and the cellar passed with Montana to Allied Domecq in 2001 and with Allied Domecq to Pernod Ricard in 2005. TOM came from the 1995 vintage and was unveiled in 1999 with the opening of a cellar named for McDonald. It is made only in years the house judges exceptional, and for a sommelier it is the wine that ties the modern Hawke's Bay Cabernet blend to the man who first bottled the grape there.

Church Road's cellar is at Taradale, near the Mission Estate, not on the Gimblett Gravels; its fruit comes from vineyards there and in the Bridge Pa Triangle.

report: The founder, Bartholomew Steinmetz, is described rather than named: his dates were not found. His being born in Luxembourg and his land coming from the Marist brothers rest on two merchant and press accounts.
Montana's purchase is 1988 in two accounts and 1989 in Te Ara, so the story says the late 1980s. The 1936 purchase year in one account is set aside for Te Ara's 1927.
The 1949 Cabernet Sauvignon as one of the country's first commercial wines of the grape is told as told, from Te Ara and the press; the record does not call it the first.

Fermenting the Cabernet in French oak vats and the Merlot in steel rests on one vintage note (2007) and is hedged as some years; barrel time runs 18 to 27 months across the notes read, so around a year and a half.
Whether Pernod Ricard still holds the winery is not told, being volatile; ownership is told to 2005 only.
